headline: Democrats could use new power to challenge Trump’s D.C. golf project
author: Rick Maese

paragraphs.text: Democrats’ takeover of Congress could present new obstacles to President Donald Trump’s plans to overhaul East Potomac Golf Links, with lawmakers preparing to use their control of federal spending and congressional committees to scrutinize — and potentially block — parts of the project.
Some Democrats are considering acting even sooner.

Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations subcommittee that oversees the Interior Department and National Park Service, said lawmakers are discussing whether restrictions on the golf project could be included in spending legislation during the lame-duck session that begins next week.

“There would certainly be an opportunity to insert some language regarding the golf course and stopping the president’s project if we can get some agreement from the Republicans,” Pingree said in an interview.

The federal government is operating under a temporary spending measure that expires Dec. 11, and Congress has not completed a full-year spending bill for the Interior Department and Park Service. That leaves lawmakers facing another funding deadline during the lame duck — and potentially, an opening for Democrats to seek restrictions on Trump’s plans.

If Republicans seek to finish the spending bill before Democrats take over, Pingree said Democrats could press for restrictions on East Potomac as part of the negotiations. If Congress instead extends temporary funding into next year, Democrats would take control with the Interior spending bill still unfinished — giving them greater power to impose restrictions, but also giving the administration more time to advance the project.
“We’ve been talking a little bit about language that we could do in the lame duck for that very purpose,” she said.

The shift in power could also complicate other high-profile projects Trump has pursued in Washington, including his White House ballroom and proposed monumental arch near Arlington Memorial Bridge. Democrats have challenged the projects’ funding, approval and contracting processes and, beginning in January, will control committees with the power to issue subpoenas, conduct investigations and pursue restrictions on federal spending.
Pingree said she wants to block the arch before construction begins but was more circumspect about the partially built ballroom, saying it would be harder to undo construction already underway.
“If we need lawsuits to do it, if we need to use subpoena power, investigative power, we’ll use every tool in our toolbox,” Pingree said.

Pingree said Democratic control of the House would also give lawmakers standing to pursue litigation over Trump’s projects, providing another potential avenue for challenging them. She said Democrats also intend to use the appropriations process to restrict Trump’s projects if they are unable to do so during the lame duck.

“We will absolutely include language to block the president’s vanity projects and his moving around of funds from different places in the National Park Service, a variety of other things, including the golf course,” she said.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-California), the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, has already outlined one possible approach. Last week, he urged congressional appropriators to place restrictions on a $500 million administration request for National Park Service construction that includes work on the East Potomac seawall and World War II Memorial.

Huffman proposed barring federal money from being used for the golf-course redevelopment and requiring any East Potomac seawall funding to be spent exclusively on the seawall. Asked whether she supports those restrictions, Pingree said, “absolutely,” adding that her staff intends to work with Huffman on potential legislative language.
Other Democrats set to take gavels on committees overseeing public lands and federal spending have similarly signaled that Trump’s projects will face new scrutiny.

A spokesman for Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), who is in line to lead the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said that while committee leadership has not been finalized, Heinrich would focus on “ensuring that public lands stay in public hands.” And Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee overseeing Interior, said Democrats would seek to hold the administration accountable for its use of federal money.

“Instead of wasting folks’ hard-earned tax dollars on Trump’s ego-driven vanity projects, we should be focused on protecting our nation’s parks — not destroying them — and reversing cuts to national parks staffing,” Merkley said in a statement. “With Democrats taking back control of Congress, now is the time to hold his Administration accountable for its misuse of federal dollars and fund our parks, not the President’s pet projects.”
The emerging congressional push comes as the administration is already fighting on a separate front to make Trump’s vision for East Potomac a reality.

The administration plans to close the golf course and most of the Hains Point peninsula Nov. 15, citing in part safety problems with the deteriorating seawall. Preservation groups asked U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes on Thursday to block the closure, arguing that the stated safety concerns are a pretext for clearing the way for Trump’s planned championship golf course. Reyes is scheduled to consider the request Nov. 13.
Trump’s plans at East Potomac are also subject to review by the National Capital Planning Commission, whose composition will change when Democrats take control of Congress.

Two of the commission’s 12 seats belong to congressional committee leaders — the chairs of the House Oversight Committee and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Those seats are held by Republicans but are expected to shift in January to Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) and Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), who are in line to lead the committees.

The potential significance of those two seats was illustrated Thursday night, when the commission voted 8-4 to approve Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch. The four commissioners representing the District opposed the project, while the eight other commissioners supported it. Had the two congressional representatives joined the District commissioners in opposition, the vote would have been deadlocked, 6-6 — not enough votes to approve the project.

East Potomac is headed for review by the same commission. The administration’s plan is expected to be presented at its Dec. 3 meeting but would not likely receive a vote for final approval until after the revamped commission is in place.

Pingree acknowledged that Democrats may be racing against an administration eager to advance several projects before the new Congress takes office. She said actions taken in the coming weeks could make some changes harder to reverse.
“It’s a little harder when he’s cutting down trees on the golf course to put them back,” she said. “But we will use whatever powers we have.”
